extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and researchers (historians, physicians, psychologists) interested in evaluating human testimony and sensory-based evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for judging the reliability of sensory observations, eyewitness and historical testimony, and for designing/assessing demonstrations of physical phenomena (sound/wave experiments). Emphasizes sensory limits, subjective perception, experimental aids, and deductive evaluation of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The senses are narrowly defined and open but a few 'rooms' in Nature; vision responds only to a small band of ether vibrations and is limited in distance and magnitude; hearing only to a limited frequency range; touch is limited to contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a baseline criterion when evaluating any sensory report: be aware that ordinary human senses miss vast portions of phenomena (e.g., wavelengths beyond visible light, very low/high audio frequencies, very small or distant objects). The telescope and microscope extend but do not remove these limits. Example specifics from the text: vision responds to ~400–790 trillion undulations/sec; hearing roughly 32–100,000 vibrations/sec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses Give Fragmentary, Surface-only Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the senses we perceive only surfaces or small portions of objects (e.g., when looking at a chair one sees only the surface turned toward one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume sensory input equals full knowledge of an object's nature. When assessing testimony or observation, account for the fact that observers only perceive limited aspects and may lack access to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses May Deceive — Distinguish Subjective from Objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The brain, not the sense-organs alone, creates perceptions; it can modify impressions or originate impressions without external objects, so subjective visions may be indistinguishable from objective ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat raw sensory reports with caution; require external corroboration or instruments to separate subjective impressions from objective facts. The text notes that large groups can simultaneously see the same subjective visions under certain conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and Expectation-induced Delusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations that excite awe, wonder, reverence, fear, or expectation are liable to produce subjective visions and delusions, sometimes simultaneously in many people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony arising from highly emotional contexts, apply extra skepticism and seek independent corroboration. The page warns that such emotional arousal can produce absolute and absurd delusions even in sane, intelligent observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrence of Many Observers Is Not Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: That many honest and intelligent people 'see' the same thing is no necessary evidence of the existence of that object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of multiple witnesses by deductive reasoning from the known circumstances under which the claims were made and from previously established scientific principles, rather than relying on mere concurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Testimony by Known Circumstances and Scientific Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of what individuals or multitudes see are to be determined, if at all, only by reasoning deductively from the known circumstances under which the claims were made and from general principles of science previously established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use context analysis and established science as primary evaluative tools. The text emphasizes that some claims may be beyond scientific investigation and must be judged against the circumstances and principles applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and Controversial Writings Are Often Unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Much historical and controversial literature contains statements 'scientifically of no value' and may be largely counterfeit of human experience; many histories should be regarded with skepticism and sometimes as fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical criticism, winnow subjective/legendary material from objective facts; prefer corroborated evidence and be skeptical of detailed narratives filtered through non-experts over centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer Expectation and Training Can Produce False Perceptions (Observer Bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation, training, or the desire to find a phenomenon can cause observers to hear or perceive what they expect (e.g., medical students hearing imagined chest sounds; anxious persons 'hearing' distant footsteps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for expectation and confirmation bias in observations and experiments. When possible, blind observers or use controls to prevent self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental/Aided Observation Should Supplement the Senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental demonstration of waves and vibrations benefits from instruments and visual/auditory aids (e.g., attach a mirror to a tuning-fork and reflect light to show vibration; use a blackened cylinder for wavy records; Weinhold's slit method to visualize particle motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer and require instrumentally aided demonstrations to make invisible processes evident and to reduce reliance on unaided senses. The page gives concrete methods for visualizing sound-wave phenomena as examples of good experimental practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate Attributes of Sound: Pitch, Amplitude, Timbre
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch relates to wave length/period (short waves = high pitch, long waves = low pitch); amplitude relates to loudness but not pitch; timbre (tone/quality) is the attribute that makes the same pitch sound different across instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing auditory evidence or experiments, treat pitch, loudness, and timbre as distinct variables to be measured or controlled. Recognize that matching pitch alone does not imply the same quality or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Dismiss Subjective Medical Symptoms Solely Because They Lack Observable Lesions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many important medical conditions (nervous exhaustion, hypochondriasis, hysteria, hay-fever, allied nervous affections) are of scientific and practical interest despite lack of observable lesions; they require deductive reasoning and patient statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In clinical evaluation, take subjective patient testimony seriously when objective signs are absent; use careful reasoning and context to assess such reports rather than automatic dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science Should Make the Senses Servants of Reason — Prefer Deduction and Calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in the evolution of great science is cutting loose from the rule of the senses, making them servants instead of kings; reason and calculation extend beyond what senses alone can provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize theoretical reasoning, measurement, and calculation when evaluating claims; use sensory data as inputs to deductive frameworks rather than as final proof. Examples cited include Copernican and gravitational theories arising from deduction beyond raw sense-data.
